# Roles and the mode contract

DW-Production is a relay. Upstream agencies publish their statistics; a Database Manager refreshes caches and produces deposited indicators; an auditor reproduces those outputs and files findings; and a publisher pushes approved data packages to UNICEF's data warehouse and the public pages that draw on it. Each runner touches a different part of the filesystem and carries a different obligation. The toolkit names the three runners **PRODUCER**, **REVIEWER** and **PUBLISHER**, and it does not rely on discipline alone to keep them apart: a session in reviewer mode is prevented in code from writing canonical artefacts (the single authoritative copy of the data everyone downstream trusts) and from calling live APIs.

This chapter sets out the three roles, what each may read and write, how the `dw_mode` session setting turns those policies into mechanical guarantees, and the second setting beside it: the project's collaboration model.

Two terms recur. A **deposit** is a finished data package a producer places in the canonical store. A deposit is **blessed** once it has passed the producer's pre-deposit checklist and the reviewer's compare report; only blessed deposits may be published.

## The three roles

Each role has a short acronym used in the repository's internal documentation; this chapter uses the plain names.

| Role | Acronym | Plain meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **PRODUCER** | DBM (Database Manager) | Owns the deposit. Refreshes upstream caches and produces the deposited indicator outputs. |
| **REVIEWER** | DBR (Database Reviewer) | Reproduces and validates. Audits, finds bugs, gathers sector-lead sign-off. |
| **PUBLISHER** | DBP (Database Publisher) | Pushes blessed deposits into the canonical UNICEF data warehouse and downstream surfaces. |

All three use the same helpers (`dw_save`, `dw_use`, `dw_api_fetch`, `dw_compare` and the rest) and the same path globals, derived from the user's profile. What differs is the slice of the filesystem each may read and write, and whether it may reach the network at all.

## What each role may read and write

| Role | Reads from | Writes to | API calls | Owns |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PRODUCER** | upstream APIs + the canonical deposit (`060.DW-MASTER`) | the canonical deposit (Teams, and the Z: mirror automatically) | **yes** | refreshing cached upstream data; producing the deposited outputs |
| **REVIEWER** | the canonical deposit (read only) + own sandbox | the sandbox only (`sandboxRoot`, per user) | **no**, forbidden by the reviewer-mode guard | reproducibility validation; sector-lead sign-off; finding bugs |
| **PUBLISHER** | the blessed work-data deposit (`013_wrkdata`) | the data warehouse: Helix, SDMX endpoints, data.unicef.org, SoWC tables | reads warehouse endpoints only | publication into the warehouse and downstream surfaces |

The deposit folders are numbered by lifecycle stage under one root, `060.DW-MASTER/01_dw_prep`: `011_rawdata` holds upstream pulls, including the `_apis/` cache, and `013_wrkdata` holds finished, promoted deposits. The numbering is a sequence (raw input becomes work data), not a count. The full path table for each mode is in [Profiles and the mode switch](profiles-and-modes.qmd).

Three things follow. Only the producer touches upstream: reviewers read the frozen caches the producer deposited. The reviewer reads canonical but writes sandbox: its reads fall back to the deposit (with a Z: integrity check), and an attempted canonical write fails. And the publisher consumes only blessed outputs from `013_wrkdata`, never raw or staging paths.

### What each role must not do

The same boundaries, seen from the other side:

| Role | Forbidden |
|---|---|
| **PRODUCER** | skip the pre-deposit checklist; deposit without a compare-vs-prior-vintage report; deposit without sector-lead sign-off on non-trivial deltas |
| **REVIEWER** | write to canonical paths; call external APIs; modify caches in the deposit |
| **PUBLISHER** | promote outputs that have not passed the producer's checklist and the reviewer's compare; publish without a provenance chain back to the original API fetches; roll back without amending the source |

The producer's prohibitions are *procedural*: enforced by checklist and review, not by code. The reviewer's are *mechanical*: enforced by `dw_mode`, as the next section shows. The publisher's are mostly procedural, with one mechanical exception: `dw_publish` refuses reviewer-mode calls (see [The publisher and `dw_publish`](#the-publisher-and-dw_publish)).

## The data flow

A single indicator moves through the relay like this:

```
External APIs                 (UIS · SDMX · WB · ILO · UNSD)
  │  PRODUCER: dw_api_fetch(refresh = TRUE)
  ▼
API cache  ── 011_rawdata/_apis ───────────────────────────┐
  │                                                          │ REVIEWER: dw_api_cached
  ▼                                                          │ (cache reads only, no live calls)
Sector pipeline  ◄─────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │  PRODUCER: dw_save(isid = ...)            REVIEWER: writes routed to sandbox
  ▼                                                   │
Canonical deposit ── 013_wrkdata ── carbon copy ──► Z: mirror (integrity check)
  │  │  ▲                                               ▲
  │  │  └── REVIEWER: dw_use (read only) ───────────────┘
  │  │            │
  │  │            ▼
  │  │     Compare report ──► Issues filed to PRODUCER / sector lead
  │  │
  └──┴── PUBLISHER ──► Helix · SDMX endpoints · data.unicef.org · SoWC / SI tables
```

The reviewer's arrows are read only; the publisher's fan out from the blessed `013_wrkdata` deposit. The diagram shows why enforcement matters: the reviewer's pipeline runs the *same scripts* as the producer's, so the only thing between an audit run and a corrupted deposit is the mode contract redirecting every write.

## How `dw_mode` enforces the boundaries

The producer/reviewer split is one session-level setting, `dw_mode`, which each person sets to `producer` or `reviewer` in their own `~/.config/user_config.yml`. It has no default, because defaulting either way is unsafe. From it the profile derives the path globals: the working globals (`teamsWrkData`, `teamsRawData`) point at the deposit for a producer and at the sandbox for a reviewer, the `*Canonical` aliases always point at the deposit, and `dw_apis_allowed` is true only for a producer. So the same scripts write to the deposit in one mode and to the sandbox in the other. How the mode is set and resolved, and the derivation, are in [Profiles and the mode switch](profiles-and-modes.qmd).

Routing paths at the profile is the first layer. The write and fetch helpers then check the mode *again* at the call site, so a script that builds a canonical path by hand, or calls the network directly, is still stopped. Two guards do this work.

### Guard 1: reviewer mode forbids canonical and Z: writes (`dw_save`)

{{< include ../_generated/badges/dw_save.md >}}

When `dw_save` is asked to write under the canonical deposit or under the Z: mirror, and the session is in reviewer mode, it refuses. The single escape hatch is `allow_canonical_write`, meant for a Database Manager's bootstrap, never for routine reviewer work.

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### R {.unnumbered .unlisted}
```r
# Reviewer-mode session. This canonical path raises an error.
dw_save(df, file.path(teamsWrkDataCanonical, "dw_im.csv"), isid = c("iso3", "year"))
#> Error: [cso_toolkit.dw_save] Reviewer mode forbids writes to canonical (Teams) deposit: .../dw_im.csv
#>  Reviewer sessions must keep canonical / Z: deposits read-only to preserve vintage permanence; writes go to the local repo sandbox.
#>  Fix:
#>  1. Resolve a sandbox path instead (the profile's `teamsWrkData` should point there in reviewer mode), OR
#>  2. If this is a deliberate Database Manager bootstrap, pass `allow_canonical_write = TRUE`.

# Producer bootstrap (rare): explicit opt-in bypasses the guard.
dw_save(df, canonical_path, isid = c("iso3", "year"), allow_canonical_write = TRUE)
```

#### Python {.unnumbered .unlisted}
```python
# Reviewer-mode session. This canonical path raises PermissionError,
# with the same Why and Fix as in R.
dw_save(df, os.path.join(teams_wrk_data_canonical, "dw_im.csv"), isid=["iso3", "year"])
# PermissionError: [cso_toolkit.dw_save] Reviewer mode forbids writes to
#   canonical (Teams) deposit: .../dw_im.csv

dw_save(df, canonical_path, isid=["iso3", "year"], allow_canonical_write=True)
```

#### Stata {.unnumbered .unlisted}
```stata
* In reviewer mode $teamsWrkData points at the sandbox, so this lands there:
dw_save , filename("dw_im.dta") path("$teamsWrkData") idvars(iso3 year)

* A path under $teamsWrkDataCanonical, $teamsRawDataCanonical or $dwZDrive
* stops with error 459:
*   [cso_toolkit.dw_save] Reviewer mode forbids writes to canonical (Teams)
*   deposit [<root>]. Pass -allow_canonical_write- to override (DBM bootstraps only).
dw_save , filename("dw_im.dta") path("$teamsWrkDataCanonical") ///
    idvars(iso3 year) allow_canonical_write
```
:::

R and Python guard a few more roots than Stata does; the exact list is in [Appendix C](../appendices/c-error-taxonomy.qmd).

::: {.callout-note}
In R and Python the same guard also runs a *producer-side* pre-flight: in producer mode, a non-canonical (sandbox) write needs at least one of the Teams or Z: mirrors to be reachable, so a deposit never ends up living only on the producer's laptop. Producer outputs are redundant by design. Every producer write fans out to both mirrors when they are available, and the Z: carbon copy is what later lets a reviewer check that Teams equals Z:.
:::

### Guard 2: reviewer mode forbids live API calls (`dw_require_no_api`)

{{< include ../_generated/badges/dw_require_no_api.md >}}

The second guard sits at every entry point that would reach the network. There are two of them:

- **`dw_api_fetch`** reads the cache first. Only when there is no cache (or the producer passed `refresh = TRUE`) does it check `dw_apis_allowed`, before any HTTP request; in reviewer mode it stops with the `[cso_toolkit.dw_api]` envelope. A reviewer reads the frozen cache with `dw_api_cached` instead.
- **`dw_require_no_api`** is the explicit assertion for any script that reaches a remote without going through `dw_api_fetch`. Call it at the top of such a script. In a Stata pipeline it is the only check there is, so call it before every network operation.

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### R {.unnumbered .unlisted}
```r
# At the top of a script that calls a remote directly
# (dw_require_no_api is defined by the generated profile):
dw_require_no_api(context = "ed/06_pull_uis")
#> Error: [X] External API access is forbidden in reviewer mode. Context: ed/06_pull_uis

# dw_api_fetch with no cache, in reviewer mode:
dw_api_fetch("uis", cache_key = "uis_entrance_age_primary")
#> Error: [cso_toolkit.dw_api] Reviewer mode forbids live API calls.
#>   Call:   dw_api_fetch('uis', cache_key='uis_entrance_age_primary')
#>   Reason: cache missing at .../_apis/uis/uis_entrance_age_primary.csv
#>   Fix:
#>     1. The expected workflow is that a Database Manager has already populated the cache under teamsRawDataCanonical/_apis/. Verify the cache file exists at the path above.
#>     2. If you ARE the producer, switch modes: set dw_mode: producer in user_config.yml and re-source the profile.

# Read the frozen cache instead:
dw_api_cached("uis", cache_key = "uis_entrance_age_primary")
```

#### Python {.unnumbered .unlisted}
```python
dw_require_no_api(context="ed/06_pull_uis")   # defined by the generated profile
# PermissionError: [X] External API access is forbidden in reviewer mode. Context: ed/06_pull_uis

# dw_api_fetch with no cache raises PermissionError with the same envelope
# as R; only fix 2 differs: _state.configure(dw_mode="producer", dw_apis_allowed=True)
dw_api_cached("uis", cache_key="uis_entrance_age_primary")
```

#### Stata {.unnumbered .unlisted}
```stata
* Assert the contract just before a live network call:
dw_require_no_api , context("ed/06_pull_uis")
* Reviewer mode aborts with error 459:
*   [cso_toolkit.dw_require_no_api] Reviewer mode forbids live API calls
*     (context: ed/06_pull_uis).
*   Why: reviewer sessions must read frozen producer caches to preserve
*     vintage permanence; any live API call breaks provenance.
*   Fix: switch the call to dw_use() against the frozen cache, or
*     re-run in producer mode.
```
:::

All of these block in reviewer mode and pass silently for a producer. `dw_api_fetch` and the Stata `dw_require_no_api` raise the toolkit's full envelope; the profile-defined R and Python `dw_require_no_api` prints a one-line `[X]` message, since it is the profile's helper rather than the package's ([Profiles and the mode switch](profiles-and-modes.qmd) shows its definition).

::: {.callout-warning}
The Stata guard has a subtlety: an **unset** mode passes. It blocks only when `$dw_mode` is `"reviewer"`; `"producer"` and any empty or unknown value pass silently. This is deliberate, since a stray script never falsely blocks a producer, but it means the *profile* must set `dw_mode` correctly. The no-default rule closes the gap: an unconfigured session stops when the profile loads (`dw_load_config` stops with error 459), before it ever reaches a guard.
:::

## The helper subset each role uses

The same functions serve all three roles, but each role uses a different subset and gets different behaviour from them.

| Helper | PRODUCER | REVIEWER | PUBLISHER |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dw_save` | writes to the deposit (Z: mirror automatic) | sandbox writes only; canonical/Z: writes fail | reads only |
| `dw_use` | reads anywhere | reads sandbox with canonical fallback; Z: integrity check | reads `013_wrkdata` |
| `dw_api_fetch` | fetches live and caches in the deposit | reads the cache; a live fetch is blocked | n/a |
| `dw_api_inventory` | audits cache freshness | audits what is available | audits provenance before publication |
| `dw_compare` | runs on every production run | runs on every reviewer run | reads compare reports as a publication gate |
| `dw_verify_z` | confirms the mirror landed after a canonical write | verifies integrity on canonical reads | final pre-publication check |
| `dw_fetch_inputs` / `dw_check_deposit` | fetch gitignored inputs from the deposit and verify them (read only on the deposit) | same: reproduce from the deposited inputs, never write to Teams or Z: | n/a |
| `dw_read_provenance` / `dw_provenance_diff` | check each run against the previous one | confirm a reproduction is byte-identical | read the sidecars as lineage evidence |
| `dw_publish` | submits to Helix (dry-run stub today) | refused | n/a |

Which language has each helper is shown under its heading in [The IO contract](31-io.qmd) and [The external-API contract](32-external-api.qmd), and in full in [Appendix A](../appendices/a-coverage-matrix.qmd).

## The publisher and `dw_publish`

{{< include ../_generated/badges/dw_publish.md >}}

PRODUCER and REVIEWER are fully wired into the mode contract; PUBLISHER only partly. One piece of the role is code: `dw_publish(path, indicator, vintage, sector, endpoint = "helix", dry_run = TRUE)`. Where `dw_save` writes a file to the Teams folder and its Z: mirror, `dw_publish` submits a file that already exists to Helix through its API; calling the canonical write "publish" confuses the two.

It already enforces the call-site contract: a reviewer-mode call stops before any I/O (`[cso_toolkit.dw_publish] Reviewer mode forbids API submissions to 'helix'.`); `path`, `indicator`, `vintage` and `sector` must each be a single non-empty string; the artefact must exist on disk; and the endpoint allowlist admits only `"helix"`.

What it does *not* yet do is submit. It is a dry-run stub: `dry_run = TRUE` validates the call and returns `status = "dry_run"` with the payload a live submission would send, including the file's `sha256`; `dry_run = FALSE` stops with an envelope pointing at issue #15, where the Helix endpoint contract is being negotiated with sector leads. The publisher's transport (to Helix, SDMX, the data portal and the SoWC tables) and its other boundaries are still enforced by procedure and review: a contract honoured mostly by hand, with the mechanical version arriving one helper at a time.

## Collaboration model: single- and multi-producer projects

Everything above assumes one producer per deposit. Co-authored research projects do not work like that: several people produce code and results, and who produces and who reviews changes over time. JP produces while Karen reviews, and a month later they swap. The toolkit handles this with a second setting beside `dw_mode` rather than inside it.

### Modes are per session; the collaboration model is per project

{{< include ../_generated/badges/dw_collaboration.md >}}

| Setting | Question | Where it lives | Who sets it | Values |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `dw_mode` | Is *this session* producing or reviewing? | `~/.config/user_config.yml` (personal, never committed) | each person, as often as their role changes | `producer`, `reviewer` |
| `collaboration` | How many people may *produce* in this project? | `cso_project.yml` at the repository root (committed) | the project, in one reviewed commit | `single-producer`, `multi-producer` |

A missing `cso_project.yml` means `single-producer`, so existing projects need no change. The file is short (template: `templates/cso_project.yml`):

```yaml
schema: cso_project/1
collaboration: multi-producer
collaboration_since: 2026-11-20
members:          # optional, informational
  - jpazevedo
  - kbarnes
```

The toolkit finds it by walking up from the `root` you pass, the profile's `rootFolder` or the working directory, and stops at the repository root, so a repository without the file never picks up a parent folder's. The model is resolved once per session and `dw_collaboration()` returns it. A new repository chooses its model when it is created ([Starting a repository](40-new-repository.qmd)).

### Why not a third mode or a new role

The obvious alternative was a third session mode (say, `co-producer`) or a fourth role. It was rejected because a mode cannot be coordinated. Modes are per person, set in a file nobody else sees. If the number of producers were a mode, two co-authors could run under different rules on the same outputs, and a producer session that knew nothing of the other producer would overwrite their work without a trace. The number of producers is a fact about the project, so it belongs in the repository: the same for everyone, changed in one reviewed commit, with a history. Modes keep their meaning.

### What `multi-producer` changes

Only `dw_save()` behaves differently, and only for an output that already exists and has a provenance sidecar. Reviewer sessions write to their sandbox and are not affected.

1. **Out-of-band change.** If the file's SHA-256 no longer matches the `sha256` in its sidecar, someone changed it without `dw_save()`; replacing it would discard a change nobody recorded, so `dw_save()` stops. A text output that differs only in line endings (a Windows clone with `core.autocrlf=true` checks tracked files out with CRLF) is not a change: `dw_save()` prints a note instead. `output/** -text` in `.gitattributes`, which the scaffolders write, keeps tracked outputs byte-exact.
2. **Concurrent write.** If the sidecar says another user wrote the file *after this session started*, two producers may be writing the same output at once, and one would silently overwrite the other, so `dw_save()` stops. The exception is an output whose file and sidecar are committed and unmodified in git: that write reached this session through a pull or merge, so this one builds on it. Outputs outside git, such as deposits, keep the check.
3. **Otherwise it writes.** When the previous writer was someone else, it prints a note, not an error. Handing the producer role back and forth is normal; a guard that fired on every handover would teach people to override it without reading it.

Either stop can be overridden with `takeover = TRUE` once you have checked what happened, and the override is recorded in the new sidecar. Every sidecar written in a multi-producer project also records its lineage (the previous writer's hash, user and time, and the git branch and commit); the fields are in [Appendix B](../appendices/b-provenance-schema.qmd). Single-producer sidecars are unchanged.

The API cache follows the same rule. An existing cache is read, never replaced, unless the producer passes `refresh = TRUE`; in a multi-producer project a refresh over another user's fetch says so and keeps the previous fetch (`metadata.previous_fetch`) in the new provenance.

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### R {.unnumbered .unlisted}
```r
dw_collaboration()
#> [1] "multi-producer"

# Karen changed the file by hand after her last dw_save():
dw_save(df, path = "outputs/table2.csv", overwrite = TRUE, force = TRUE)
#> Error: [cso_toolkit.dw_save] Multi-producer project: refusing to replace outputs/table2.csv.
#>  Why (out-of-band change): the file's SHA-256 (5e1f0c...) no longer matches its
#>  provenance sidecar (a07c9b...): someone changed it without dw_save(), so
#>  replacing it now would discard a change nobody recorded.
#>  Fix:
#>  1. Reconcile first: sync or pull the other change, check the file's history
#>     (git log, the sidecar's user and written_at), and re-run, OR
#>  2. If you have checked it and mean to replace it, pass `takeover = TRUE`;
#>     the takeover is recorded in the new sidecar.

dw_save(df, path = "outputs/table2.csv", overwrite = TRUE, force = TRUE,
        takeover = TRUE)
```

#### Python {.unnumbered .unlisted}
```python
dw_collaboration()
# 'multi-producer'

dw_save(df, path="outputs/table2.csv", overwrite=True)
# PermissionError: [cso_toolkit.dw_save] Multi-producer project: refusing to
#   replace outputs/table2.csv.
#   Why (out-of-band change): ...
#   Fix: ... pass `takeover=True`; the takeover is recorded in the new sidecar.

dw_save(df, path="outputs/table2.csv", overwrite=True, takeover=True)
```

#### Stata {.unnumbered .unlisted}
```stata
* The same guards, through Stata's Python integration (Stata 16+):
dw_collaboration                       // $dw_collaboration_model, once per session
dw_save, filename(table2) path("outputs") idvars(iso3 year)
* [cso_toolkit.dw_save] Multi-producer project: refusing to replace ...
*   Fix: ... pass -takeover-; the takeover is recorded in the new sidecar.
dw_save, filename(table2) path("outputs") idvars(iso3 year) takeover
* Without Python a multi-producer write stops unless -takeover- is passed.
```
:::

### How to switch, and why switching midway is safe

{{< include ../_generated/badges/dw_set_collaboration.md >}}

Switch with `dw_set_collaboration()`, never by editing the file alone, and commit the result as one pull request that a co-author reviews:

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### R {.unnumbered .unlisted}
```r
dw_set_collaboration("multi-producer", root = rootFolder,
                     members = c("jpazevedo", "kbarnes"))
#> [cso_toolkit.dw_set_collaboration] wrote .../cso_project.yml: collaboration = multi-producer
#> [cso_toolkit.dw_set_collaboration] baselined 37 of 37 provenance sidecar(s) under ...
```

#### Python {.unnumbered .unlisted}
```python
dw_set_collaboration("multi-producer", root=root_folder,
                     members=["jpazevedo", "kbarnes"])
```
:::

The call writes `cso_project.yml` and adds a `baseline` object (`collaboration`, `at`, `by`) to every existing `*.provenance.json` under the root, inserted as text so `sha256` and every other field keep their bytes. It refuses to run in reviewer mode, because it writes, and a second call changes nothing. Switching back is the same call with the other value.

The switch is a non-event for three reasons:

- **No mixed rules.** The setting is in the repository, so every collaborator moves to the new rules at the same commit, when they pull it.
- **No flood of alarms.** The baseline marks artefacts produced before the switch as project-owned, so the first multi-producer write over each is quiet instead of reporting a change of producer.
- **No lineage gap.** The baseline leaves `sha256` untouched, so the first multi-producer write records it as `previous_sha256`, and the chain starts from the last single-producer state of each file.

### A worked example: two co-authors who swap roles

JP and Karen co-author a paper in one repository. Until now JP has produced every table; Karen has reviewed.

1. **The switch.** Karen will produce the robustness tables, so JP runs `dw_set_collaboration("multi-producer", ...)` in a producer session and opens a pull request with `cso_project.yml` and the baselined sidecars. Karen reviews and merges it.
2. **Karen produces.** She sets her own `dw_mode` to `producer`, pulls and re-runs `03_robustness.R`. Her first write over `table3.csv`, last written by JP, is quiet because the sidecar carries a baseline; the new sidecar records JP's hash as `previous_sha256`.
3. **JP reviews.** He sets his `dw_mode` to `reviewer` and reproduces her tables in his sandbox. No guard is involved.
4. **They overlap by accident.** Both run `02_main.R` in producer mode on the shared folder. Karen's run finishes first, so when JP's reaches `dw_save()` for `table2.csv` the sidecar shows a write after his session started, and it stops. JP pulls, compares, and either re-runs or passes `takeover = TRUE`, which is recorded.
5. **The roles swap back.** A month later JP's first write over a table Karen last wrote prints a note ("last written by kbarnes; your write follows theirs in its lineage") and proceeds.

Neither changed the project setting again: who produces is a session matter; how many may produce was settled once, in review. A new co-author needs only their personal block in `user_config.yml`, with `dw_mode: reviewer` until they start producing; the project file decides the rest, and they could not override it there if they tried.

## Why this matters

The point of the relay is *reproducibility with permanence*. A reviewer must run the producer's exact scripts and get the producer's exact numbers, which means reading the same frozen caches (each a *vintage*: the data as they stood when the producer pulled them), never a fresher pull from a live API that has moved on. And the reviewer must do so without any risk of overwriting the deposit under audit. The API guard keeps the reviewer on frozen vintages; the `dw_save` guard keeps the reviewer's output in a sandbox. Set `dw_mode` once, and the same code base behaves as a producer or as a reviewer, without editing a single sector script.
